batch.title: Wetland management: findings that move a rating (first check)
batch.notes: Every wetland management finding that no person has checked yet and that would change a rating if it were wrong. Each card says what the paper says, what we recorded and what looks wrong (or that it checks out), and what Approve or Reject would change today (trial run, 10 Nov). The AI's suggested call shows under the buttons; it is a suggestion only. Approve = recorded correctly, stays in use. Hold = leave it open with a note. Reject = set aside (kept on record, no longer counted); pick a reason.

units.citation: Acreman et al. (2013). How Wetlands Affect Floods. Wetlands.
units.quote:
Modelling of the River Cherwell, UK (Acreman et al. 2003), 
showed that construction of embankments would remove flood water storage and increase the 
peak flow downstream near the city of Oxford by 57% (Figure 6).

relationship.outcome_raw: construction of embankments would remove floodplain flood-water storage and increase the peak flow downstream near the city by 57 per cent

context.practice_as_described: narrative review of how wetland type, landscape position and MANAGEMENT (drainage, drain blocking, re-vegetation, embanking and de-embanking floodplains, controlling ditch water levels) change flood generation and attenuation
context.note: LOSS frame and the strongest quantified floodplain-reconnection signal in this lane: disconnecting the floodplain raises the downstream peak, so reconnecting it lowers one. Modelled, not measured

units.question: Acreman 2013 reports a model of the River Cherwell, UK: building embankments that cut the river off from its floodplain would raise the flood peak downstream by 57%. We recorded this as the reverse case: reconnecting the floodplain lowers flood peaks, a strong effect, modelled. It is an older study by the same author, retold. Looks right. Approve keeps it. Reject: flood benefit for wetland restoration and rewetting drops from moderate to slight; the mixed-income lines keep 'conflicting' but confidence falls from low to very low. AI's view: Number and direction are in the quote and it is correctly marked as modelled and as a loss-of-floodplain case.

units.question: Acreman 2013 retells a Welsh field study (Wilson 2011): after drains in a blanket bog were blocked, flows and flood peaks fell in the drains and hill streams. units.quote:
A 
change of vegetation from wet meadows to the shrubs and trees can double the size and depth 
of the inundated area for the same size of the flood (Swiatek et al. 2008).

relationship.outcome_raw: changing floodplain vegetation from wet meadow to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the inundated area for a flood of the same size

context.practice_as_described: narrative review of how wetland type, landscape position and MANAGEMENT (drainage, drain blocking, re-vegetation, embanking and de-embanking floodplains, controlling ditch water levels) change flood generation and attenuation
context.note: STAGE versus PEAK, in one sentence: the roughness that cuts the downstream peak RAISES water level and flooded area locally. A flood row that reports only peak attenuation hides the local stage cost to the landholder whose floodplain is being re-roughened

units.question: Acreman 2013, retelling Swiatek 2008, says a change from wet meadow to shrubs and trees can double the size and depth of the flooded area. We recorded it as wetland restoration making floods strongly worse. The page is a general passage on how vegetation roughness works; it does not say anyone restored anything. Approve keeps it as the main harm finding. Reject: mixed-income flood lines move from 'conflicting' to low or slight benefit; overall flood benefit confidence rises from high to very high. AI's view: The quote describes vegetation change in general, not a restoration action, yet it carries a strong harm vote.

units.quote:
They calculated that raising water levels in ditches in one of the catchments to meet 
ecological targets in winter would result in the loss of flood water storage volume equivalent 
to 3% of the medium annual flood volume.

relationship.outcome_raw: raising winter water levels in the ditches of a floodplain fen wetland to meet ecological targets would cost flood-water storage volume equivalent to 3 per cent of the median annual flood volume

context.practice_as_described: narrative review of how wetland type, landscape position and MANAGEMENT (drainage, drain blocking, re-vegetation, embanking and de-embanking floodplains, controlling ditch water levels) change flood generation and attenuation
context.note: REVERSAL kept and it is the one that most threatens a naive wetland flood row: REWETTING a floodplain wetland fills the storage that would otherwise absorb a flood. Wet wetlands and empty flood storage are competing objectives, and the review says so explicitly in its conclusions

units.question: Acreman 2013 reports a Somerset study: raising ditch water levels in winter for wildlife would use up flood storage equal to 3% of the typical annual flood. We recorded rewetting making floods slightly worse, modelled. Looks right: the number and the 'would' are both there. Approve keeps this trade-off. Reject: mixed-income flood lines stay 'conflicting' but confidence falls from low to very low. AI's view: A genuine, modest trade-off, correctly marked slight and modelled.

units.quote:
Notably, river and floodplain management (RFM) 
demonstrated higher effectiveness, achieving an average flood peak reduction of 30%, particularly in larger catchments.

relationship.outcome_raw: flood PEAK reduction (not stage), river and floodplain management measure group averaged across reviewed case studies; wetland restoration is only a component of the bundle

context.practice_as_described: river and floodplain management (RFM): 'river restoration, floodplain/wetland restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage areas' — floodplain/wetland restoration listed as 'Floodplain reconnection, restoration of the natural pools ... embankment removal and restoring wetlands'
context.note: systematic review of 145 papers / 216 case studies, 79% Europe and ~55% UK (p3) - income_group high, country not set; PEAK not stage; RFM reductions range from 1% to 75% across return periods (p20-21, sentence straddles the page break, unquotable); empirical monitoring dominates small catchments and modelling larger ones (abstract) so this average mixes measured and modelled; no position-in-catchment split; authors note NFM can synchronise sub-basin peaks and worsen downstream flooding (p7, citing Odoni 2010) and that RFM effectiveness may decline over time (p21) - both generic NFM, not emitted

units.question: Bagheri 2025, a review of 145 papers, says river and floodplain management cut flood peaks by 30% on average. We recorded a strong flood benefit for wetland restoration. But that group also includes river restoration, leaky barriers and offline storage ponds, so the 30% is not wetland restoration alone; most cases are UK and part are models. Approve keeps it strong. Reject: flood benefit for wetland restoration and rewetting drops from moderate to slight. AI's view: The 30% average mixes leaky dams and storage ponds with wetland work, so crediting all of it to wetland restoration overstates.

units.quote:
Under the Lake Champlain TMDL implementation plan, the Mad 
River watershed is required to reduce its P load by 68 kg/yr, or 15% of 
the annual load reduction assigned for the overall Winooski River basin 
452 kg/yr (VANR Watershed Management Vermont Agency of Natural 
Resources Watershed Management Division, 2018). Each of the sce­
narios (besides E and F) would meet this reduction when considering the 
P credit values, and each of the scenarios would meet this reduction 
when considering the predicted P storage values (Table 3).

relationship.outcome_raw: PHOSPHORUS load reduction delivered by the floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration scenarios against the watershed's regulatory load-reduction requirement - every scenario met the requirement on predicted P storage, and every scenario except E and F met it on the regulatory P-credit accounting

context.practice_as_described: 'Eleven different floodplain reconnection and wetland restoration modifications were combined in six scenarios and simulated with 2D Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System (2D HEC-RAS), along with a baseline (no-action) scenario'; the techniques named are 'revegetation, floodplain lowering, berm removal, cross culverts/bridges, or flood chute reconnection'
context.note: NET REMOVAL (storage on the floodplain), not export. The water-quality objective is met comfortably in the same scenarios where the flood-peak objective is barely moved - that trade-off is the paper's point.

units.question: The same 2022 Vermont study says most restoration scenarios would meet the river basin's phosphorus-reduction target of 68 kg a year. We recorded a nutrient-removal benefit, no size. Direction is right, but it is a simulation labelled as measured, and 'would meet a target' is a projection. Approve keeps it. Reject: the separate rain-fed cropping and upper-middle-income lines on the water quality row would no longer show, as they would then match the overall rating. AI's view: Projected phosphorus storage from a model, recorded as measured.

units.citation: Cheng et al. (2020). Maximizing US nitrate removal through wetland protection and restoration. Nature.
units.quote:
The costs for construction of new or restored wetlands were calculated 
using a cost-based decision support framework for wetland restora-
tion18,53. This framework includes area-dependent costs associated 
with design, construction and maintenance, annualized over a 50-year 
management horizon at a real discount rate of 4%. It also includes land 
rental costs, which vary by state and have been established to cover 
the opportunity costs for land removed from agricultural produc-
tion53. Land rental costs for cropland and pastureland were obtained 
at a state level from the Quick Stats 2.0 database (http://quickstats.
nass.usda.gov).
The costs of restoring 1 ha of wetland on cropland and pastureland for 
each of the 48 states in the contiguous US are shown in Extended Data 
Fig. 4. Land rental costs for cropland are, in the mean, more than five 
times greater than those for pastureland (cropland, US$274 ± 156 ha−1);

relationship.outcome_raw: annual land-rental cost per hectare of wetland restored on CROPLAND, which the authors state covers the opportunity cost of land removed from agricultural production and is more than five times the pastureland figure

context.practice_as_described: modelled scenarios that add wetland area across the contiguous US: 'Random placement' (SC1), 'No agricultural land loss' (SC2, wetlands placed only on non-agricultural lands) and 'Targeted restoration' (SC3, wetlands preferentially placed in areas with the highest N surplus). The authors state 'the costs estimated herein are for constructed nutrient retention wetlands, as exemplified by the USDA CREP wetland programme', and wetland N removal is 'the difference between N inputs and N outputs across a wetland', including plant uptake and denitrification
context.note: costs given in 2017 US dollars, annualized over a 50-year management horizon at a 4% real discount rate (stated in the quote). The pastureland comparator figure (US$51 ha-1) sits on the following page and is not contiguous in the text layer, so it is not quoted. Denominator is per hectare per year.

units.question: Cheng 2020 costs US wetland restoration; land rent for cropland taken out of farming averages US$274 per hectare per year. We recorded this as the yearly running cost of wetland creation. Note it is the land-rent part only, not design or building, and US prices. Looks right as a yearly cost. Approve keeps it. Reject: the yearly-cost line for wetland management falls to one paper with very low confidence; the creation and restoration lines drop out. AI's view: The number is in the quote and a yearly land-rent cost fits the yearly-cost row; costs carry no rating anyway.

units.question: An FAO 2024 evaluation in Laos says a weir at Nongdern wetland nearly doubled the farmland served with water, from 37 to 73 hectares. We recorded a strong water-supply benefit of wetland restoration. units.quote:
Floodplain restoration (i.e., 
bankfull floodplain reconnection and Stage 0) can also provide flood management, but 
has not been sufficiently evaluated for small frequent storms. We used 1D unsteady 
Hydrologic Engineering Center's River Analysis System to simulate small storms in a 
5 km-­long, second-­order generic stream from the Chesapeake Bay watershed, and 
varied % channel restored (starting at the upstream end), restoration location, res-
toration bank height (distinguishes bankfull from Stage 0 restoration), and floodplain 
width/Manning's n. Stream restoration decreased (attenuated) peak flow up to 37% 
and increased floodplain exchange by up to 46%.

units.citation: Pang et al. (2022). Policy Cognition, Household Income and Farmers’ Satisfaction: Evidence from a Wetland Ecological Compensation Project in the Poyang Lake Area at the Micro Level. Sustainability.
units.quote:
Of the surveyed rural households, 56.9% thought that household incomes decreased
after participating in the policy, 38.3% thought that household incomes did not change
and only 4.8% thought that household incomes increased. The results indicate that most
rural households believed that household incomes decreased after participating in the
wetland ecological compensation policy. The policy has no positive impacts on household
incomes, which is attributed to the low compensation rates for most farmers.

relationship.outcome_raw: share of surveyed households reporting that household income DECREASED after joining the wetland ecological compensation policy (most of the rest reported no change, very few an increase); the authors attribute the loss to low compensation rates

context.practice_as_described: wetland ecological compensation policies at Poyang Lake: a 2014 pilot that compensates for the ecological benefits of wetlands, alongside the national programme returning farmland to wetlands, a lake-wide fishing moratorium and migratory-bird habitat protection; compensation is paid mainly in cash to arable landowners and the community
context.note: Cross-sectional household survey, 773 households, 27 villages, July 2019; ordered-logit on policy satisfaction. Income change is the household's OWN PERCEPTION of change since joining the policy - no counterfactual, no measured income. PICOS: the paper does not separate restoration (farmland returned to wetland) from conservation compensation for existing wetland (bird-habitat protection, fishing ban), so attribution = bundled. THE TRANSFER PATTERN: the household outcome is governed by the compensation rate, not by production - here the transfer is too low to make most households whole (65.7% rate the compensation low or very low, operational unit ev_wgy_poy_op1). Corroborates Feng et al. 2024 (same lake), where transfer income was the only component that rose. Perception shares set no strength class.

units.quote:

context.practice_as_described: Bear River levee setback, Yuba and Sutter Counties, California (2005-2006): nearly 3 km of levee set back along the Bear River and a levee removed on the Feather River at the confluence, reconnecting 240 ha of floodplain; most of the setback area allowed to grow into forest, part kept as mown grassland for low hydraulic roughness, plus an excavated floodplain swale (p10-11). units.citation: Gourevitch et al. (2020). Spatial targeting of floodplain restoration to equitably mitigate flood risk. Global Environmental Change.
units.quote:
Restoring
many of the reaches along Lewis Creek has no eﬀect on property da-
mages from ﬂooding. In fact, for some reaches, restoration even wor-
sens inundation upstream through “backwater eﬀects” (see Figure S2;
Thomas and Nisbet, 2007). In some scenarios, restoration beneﬁts for
some properties were canceled out by increased ﬂood damages for
others. In other scenarios, restoration eﬀorts substantially increased
aggregate ﬂood damages over the baseline scenario.

relationship.outcome_raw: restoration at some reaches WORSENED inundation upstream through backwater effects, and in some scenarios substantially increased aggregate flood damages above the no-restoration baseline

context.practice_as_described: floodplain restoration by revegetating stream reaches that are disconnected from the adjacent floodplain: at each of 199 candidate reaches one of 'forest revegetation', 'wetland revegetation' or 'do nothing'; implemented in HEC-RAS as a change in floodplain roughness, paid for as a land easement plus revegetation labour and materials
context.note: MALADAPTATION / reversal finding, kept: direction is on flood_hazard as named, so positive = the hazard got worse; the authors warn that neglecting the spatial relationship between restoration and exposed properties 'may have severe unintended consequences'

units.citation: Stachowicz et al. (2022). To store or to drain — To lose or to gain? Rewetting drained peatlands as a measure for increasing water storage in the transboundary Neman River Basin. Science of The Total Environment.
units.quote:
Applying multiple assumptions, it was revealed that
rewetting drained peatlands in the Neman River Basin could increase water retention by 23.6–118 M m3. This corre-
sponds to 0.14–0.7% of the total annual Neman River discharge into the Baltic Sea. Unit increase of water retention
volume due to rewetting ranged between 69 and 344 m3·ha−1.

relationship.outcome_raw: additional water retained in the landscape after rewetting drained peatland (water-table rise around blocked ditches times peat porosity), per hectare; basin total equals a small fraction of annual river discharge

context.practice_as_described: rewetting of drained peatlands (fens and bogs) by blocking drainage ditches: simple ditch blocks of wood and peat (non-regulated outflow) or sophisticated blocks with water-level regulation, at stacking (damming) heights of 0.1, 0.3 or 0.5 m, across the Neman basin
context.note: Basin-scale GIS model over 8885 drained-peatland polygons, 18 scenarios (radius of water-level rise from the ditch, peat porosity, stacking height); water storage valued at reservoir replacement cost (EUR/m3/yr). Income: LTU/POL/RUS high, BLR upper-middle (most of the cost falls in Belarus). Range = mean retained volume at stacking heights 0.1 to 0.5 m (Table 1). Mechanism: blocked ditches raise the water level in the peat, which stores water in its pore space.

units.question: Stachowicz 2022 modelled that rewetting drained peat in the Neman basin could hold an extra 69 to 344 cubic metres of water per hectare. We recorded more water retained, as a model result. Looks right; the basin total is under 1% of river flow. Approve keeps it. Reject: the peatland water shortage row stays slight positive, confidence falls from very high to high. AI's view: Numbers are in the quote and it is correctly labelled as a model projection.

units.citation: Liu et al. (2024). Effectiveness assessment of China's coastal wetland ecological restoration: A meta-analysis. Science of The Total Environment.
units.quote:
According to the comparison data of 440 restored wetlands and 
degraded wetlands, the level of biodiversity is 36.8 % (lnR = 0.313, 95 
% CI = 0.241 to 0.389) higher in the restored wetlands than in the 
degraded wetlands. The data of 198 restored wetlands and reference 
wetlands show that the level of biodiversity is 10.7 % (lnR = −0.113, 95 
% CI = −0.190 to −0.040) lower in the restored wetlands than that in 
the reference wetlands (Fig. 2).

relationship.outcome_raw: biodiversity indicators (density, abundance, richness, Shannon, Simpson of vegetation, soil microbes, invertebrates, vertebrates), restored vs degraded coastal wetlands; revegetation improves the soil environment and habitat

context.practice_as_described: coastal wetland ecological restoration in China: active restoration (planting mangroves, building dikes, soil improvement, freshwater input) and passive restoration (dike breaking to restore the hydrological state, removal of invasive species) across mangroves, salt marshes, mudflats, estuaries, deltas, bays, seaweed beds, sandy coast
context.note: Meta-analysis of 78 Chinese studies (1671 observations), lnR random-effects with bootstrap CIs; restored vs degraded and restored vs reference (natural) wetlands; fail-safe N and funnel plot show no publication bias. Mechanism (p8): vegetation restoration improves the soil environment for soil microorganisms; vegetation diversity recovery is weakest, linked to monoculture planting.

units.question: Liu 2024 pooled 440 Chinese comparisons: wildlife was 36.8% higher in restored than degraded coastal wetlands. We recorded a strong gain. Numbers match. One caution: the pool includes mangrove planting, which is now a separate practice. Approve keeps it. Reject: wildlife drops from strong to moderate positive for the whole practice, for upper-middle income and for coastal wetlands; the high-income line goes because it would then match. AI's view: Significant meta-analysis result matching the quote; mangrove overlap is a caveat, not an error.

context.practice_as_described: 'returning farmland to lakes': farmers withdraw from residential areas and cultivated land formed by reclaiming land from lakes, which are restored to natural lakes on a large scale to improve the wetland ecosystem; most surveyed farmers received no continuous subsidy
context.note: balanced panel of 365 households surveyed in 2018 and 2021 around the Poyang Lake wetland; two-way fixed-effect model plus propensity-score matching (k-nearest-neighbour, kernel/'nuclear' and radius) to correct self-selection. The outcome is the natural logarithm of household income in Yuan (plus 1), so an ATT is a log difference and is read here as a log response ratio. All three matching methods agree in sign and are within a few hundredths of each other; the kernel row is used throughout for consistency. Table 2 of the same paper gives the two-way fixed-effect coefficient on total income as -0.257 (p<0.1) without controls and -0.171 (not significant) with them. The strongest measured household signal in this lane: per capita income is lower for participants at the 1% level under all three matching methods, while total household income is not — the household absorbed the loss by putting more members to work.

relationship.outcome_raw: household TRANSFER income (pensions, agricultural subsidies, ecological compensation) of farmers participating in wetland restoration, propensity-score matched (kernel matching)

context.practice_as_described: 'returning farmland to lakes': farmers withdraw from residential areas and cultivated land formed by reclaiming land from lakes, which are restored to natural lakes on a large scale to improve the wetland ecosystem; most surveyed farmers received no continuous subsidy
context.note: balanced panel of 365 households surveyed in 2018 and 2021 around the Poyang Lake wetland; two-way fixed-effect model plus propensity-score matching (k-nearest-neighbour, kernel/'nuclear' and radius) to correct self-selection. The outcome is the natural logarithm of household income in Yuan (plus 1), so an ATT is a log difference and is read here as a log response ratio. All three matching methods agree in sign and are within a few hundredths of each other; the kernel row is used throughout for consistency. Table 2 of the same paper gives the two-way fixed-effect coefficient on total income as -0.257 (p<0.1) without controls and -0.171 (not significant) with them. WHO GAINS: transfer income is the only component that rises, significantly, under every matching method. Transfer income is defined on page 7 as pensions, agricultural subsidies, ecological compensation and compensation for migrant-bird damage — so the gain is the compensation channel, not production. The paper notes most surveyed farmers received no continuous restoration subsidy and that fishing-ban compensation covered only one year.

units.question: Feng 2024, same table: 'transfer income' (pensions, subsidies, compensation payments) rose for households who returned farmland to lakes. We recorded a strong income gain. But total household income did not rise, and this part is compensation payments, not a benefit of the wetland itself. Approve keeps it. Reject: income for restoration and rewetting stays 'moderate negative' and confidence rises from high to very high. AI's view: One component (compensation payments) is recorded as an overall income gain while total income did not rise.

units.citation: Wu et al. (2023). Wetland-based solutions against extreme flood and severe drought: Efficiency evaluation of risk mitigation. Climate Risk Management.
units.quote:
(i) quantify the impacts of wetlands on extreme flood and severe drought and (2) 
investigate the influences of geographical location and types of wetlands on their regulation ef­
ficiency. The hydrological modeling was conducted with various wetland loss scenarios on the 
Nenjiang River Basin (NRB)- a large river basin where wetlands are abundant and play an 
important hydrological regulation function. Modeling results showed that RWs mainly decreased 
peak flow and reduced downstream flood volume. However, IWs predominantly decreased flood 
volume and slightly mitigated peak flow in the entire NRB. For severe drought, RWs overall

units.citation: Bullock et al. (2003). The role of wetlands in the hydrological cycle. Hydrology and Earth System Sciences.
units.quote:
There is strong evidence that wetlands evaporate more 
water that other land types, such as forests, savannah 
grassland or arable land. Two thirds of studies (48 of 
74) conclude that wetlands increase average annual 
evaporation or reduce average annual river flow. About 
10% of studies (7) conclude the opposite; for example 
some woodlands in Zambia had greater evaporation than 
the adjacent wetlands. The remaining 25% are neutral. 
There is no obvious distinction amongst different 
wetland sub-types or geographical regions of the world.

relationship.outcome_raw: the opposite (less evaporation / more annual flow than the adjacent land) in about 10% of studies (7), e.g. Zambian woodlands evaporating more than adjacent wetlands

context.practice_as_described: EXISTING freshwater wetlands of all hydrological types (floodplain and headwater; lakes excluded, p2). No intervention: studies of what existing wetlands do. context.note: Vote count of functional statements from the review's database (Table 5, pp7-8, 'number of functional statements for each wetland type'); the table's OCR is not in row/column order, so the counts are taken from the Conclusions text. The authors warn (p5) that counts are not inter-compared, that some functions are studied more than others, and that the sample is dominated by North America. Mechanism in the quote: wetlands evaporate more water than forest, savannah grassland or arable land, so less water leaves as river flow.
